# 2. Read & Practice

> "At the heart of quantitative reasoning is a single question: Compared to what?"
>
> -- Edward Tufte

The readings listed below are broken into two groups:

1. Design principles
2. Coding techniques to implement those principles

### Design principles

Comparisons come in a few flavors: comparing groups to each other, comparing a value to a benchmark, and comparing whole distributions. These readings cover when each kind of chart works (and one common chart design that almost never does):

- Wilke: [7 - Visualizing distributions](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/histograms-density-plots.html)
- Wilke: [9 - Visualizing many distributions at once](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/boxplots-violins.html)
- [Dual-Scaled Axes in Graphs - Are They Ever the Best Solution?](http://www.perceptualedge.com/articles/visual_business_intelligence/dual-scaled_axes.pdf)

### Coding techniques

The readings below each walk through how to build a specific comparison chart in ggplot. You don't need to write this code yourself, but you should read it closely enough to recognize the pieces: a dumbbell chart is just points connected by segments, a slope chart is lines between two time points, and a bullet chart is bars layered on top of a benchmark. When an agent builds one of these for you, knowing the pieces is how you spot what it got wrong.

- [Slope charts](http://r-statistics.co/Top50-Ggplot2-Visualizations-MasterList-R-Code.html#Slope%20Chart)
- [Bullet charts](https://themockup.blog/posts/2020-11-29-bullet-chart-variants-in-r/)
- [Dumbbell charts](http://uc-r.github.io/cleveland-dot-plots)

You may also want to take a look at the [top 50 ggplots](http://r-statistics.co/Top50-Ggplot2-Visualizations-MasterList-R-Code.html), which contains examples with ggplot code to create 50 common visualizations.

# 3. Extend your skill, then make a chart

Last week you built your own data visualization skill (e.g., `.claude/skills/my-dataviz/SKILL.md`). That skill was focused on amounts and proportions. This week you will teach it how to handle comparisons.

### Extend your skill

1. Open Claude Code in your course repo and ask it to help you add a section on **comparisons** to your existing skill, using the readings above as source material (you can give it the URLs). Ask it to extend the skill you already have, not write a new one.
2. **Read what it wrote.** Does the new section capture the guidance from the readings? Some things worth checking for:
   - When comparing only 2 things, does it suggest dodged bars, bullet charts, or a dumbbell? What about 3 or more?
   - Does it say when to add a reference line (like an average or a target) for context?
   - Does it say to use facets instead of piling many categories into a legend?
   - Does it rule out dual y-axes?
3. **Make it yours.** Edit the new section (directly, or by asking Claude to) so it reflects your own choices.

### Use your skill to make a chart

Find a dataset with at least one categorical variable and something worth comparing across it (two time points, two groups, or a value and a benchmark). You can use one from the [Packages](../finding-data.html#packages) section of the "Finding Data" page, or data from your project. Then ask Claude to make a **comparison** chart using your skill (invoke it with `/your-skill-name`).

Check the result against your skill and the readings. Is the comparison the reader should make the easiest one to see? If there is a reference line, is it at the right value, and is it labeled? In a dumbbell or slope chart, are the points connected to the right partners, and are the categories sorted in a meaningful order? If something is wrong, fix it, and consider whether your skill should be updated so that it gets it right next time.

In your ``r hw_file`` file, include:

- A few sentences on what you added to your skill, and what you changed after Claude drafted it.
- The chart you made with your skill, with one or two sentences under it describing what it shows.
- A few sentences on how it went: Did the chart follow your skill on the first try? What did you have to check, correct, or change in the skill?
